title: Winning the Relay Race: Long-Running Agents in High-Value Customer Journeys | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z's David Haber argues long-running AI agents can own multi-week 'relay race' customer journeys (plaintiff law, insurance, mortgages, enterprise sales) end to end, shifting AI vendors from selling cost savings to being paid on outcomes — and threatening incumbents like Red Ventures.

insights.claim: Long customer journeys such as plaintiff-law case preparation are 'relay races' with drop-off and value leakage at every handoff: slow intake lets prospects sign with the first firm that calls back, and thin attention on routine cases lowers settlement value.
insights.speaker: David Haber
insights.so_what: Map where handoffs leak value in any multi-week workflow; that is where an agent's ROI concentrates.
insights.locator: Value Only Appears At The End Of The Relay Race

insights.claim: Human capacity limits cause concrete losses in legal case work: a firm may accept a first settlement offer when a detailed read of a doctor's note would have revealed a brain injury and a higher settlement value.
insights.speaker: David Haber
insights.so_what: Illustrates why exhaustive document review by agents can raise revenue, not just cut cost.
insights.locator: Value Only Appears At The End Of The Relay Race

insights.claim: Context fragmentation across documents, stakeholders and systems over months makes it nearly impossible for humans to hold the full picture of every case, so bills get omitted from demand letters and treatment gaps go unexplained.
insights.speaker: David Haber
insights.so_what: Persistent memory is a core differentiator of long-running agents.
insights.locator: Value Only Appears At The End Of The Relay Race

insights.claim: Until recently AI agents handled bounded tasks with short interactions and verifiable outcomes (customer support was the early use case); long-running agents now pursue goals across dozens of steps, modalities and long time horizons.
insights.speaker: David Haber
insights.so_what: Agent value is migrating from narrow task automation toward whole-journey ownership; watch vendors who can demonstrate multi-week reliability.

insights.claim: A long-running case agent can wake on events or deadlines, dispatch sub-agents to call witnesses, update clients, work across phone/email/text, consolidate findings and keep learning across cases, so evidence collection is no longer bounded by human capacity.
insights.speaker: David Haber
insights.so_what: Architecture pattern: persistent context + event wake-ups + sub-agent fan-out.

insights.claim: Because agents are nearly infinitely scalable, even seemingly routine low-value cases get worked fully, which removes a labor constraint that previously forced firms to triage claims.
insights.speaker: David Haber
insights.so_what: Unit economics of low-value work flip when marginal attention costs near zero.

insights.claim: Owning the full customer journey lets AI vendors drive revenue uplift rather than only cost reduction, and because outcomes are observable and attributable they can price on work product or outcomes, reaching contract values unattainable through cost savings alone.
insights.speaker: David Haber
insights.so_what: TAM expands from a share of labor budgets to a share of revenue; favors vendors with attributable outcomes.

insights.claim: Outcome pricing faces friction: most US states bar non-lawyers from sharing legal fees, procurement teams lack precedent for outcome-based contracts, and attribution disputes will likely arise early, making deployment a commercial challenge as much as a technical one.
insights.speaker: David Haber
insights.so_what: Regulatory and procurement barriers can slow adoption in legal, regulated verticals.

insights.claim: Red Ventures pioneered end-to-end outsourced digital sales for long-term consumer contracts, e.g. owning sites like homeinsurance.com and closing policies for insurers, and per S&P Global generated about $370M EBITDA on about $1.4B sales in 2022.
insights.speaker: David Haber
insights.so_what: Benchmark for how lucrative owning a journey and being paid per close can be.
insights.locator: The Case For An AI-native Red Ventures

insights.claim: Red Ventures' model looks structurally threatened: consumers can ask personal agents such as Meta's Muse or Instinct for recommendations, devaluing traditional comparison sites, while long-running agents can replace hundreds of humans running linear funnels; its EBITDA fell to an estimated ~$160M in 2025.
insights.speaker: David Haber
insights.so_what: Lead-gen and comparison-site intermediaries are exposed to agentic discovery and agentic sales; an AI-native entrant could take the profit pool.
insights.locator: The Case For An AI-native Red Ventures

insights.claim: Three go-to-market routes exist for long-running agents: sell the platform (price upside, longer sales cycles, harder attribution), sell the service by replacing outsourced BPO work (shorter cycles, but legacy pricing and in-house journeys limit reach), or go full-stack and become the AI-native operator.
insights.speaker: David Haber
insights.so_what: Use as a lens to classify AI startups' revenue models and margin ceilings.

insights.claim: Full-stack example: instead of selling an agent to a debt collection firm, buy debt portfolios and collect them directly to capture all AI upside and solve attribution, at the cost of owning licensing and compliance outside the core journey.
insights.speaker: David Haber
insights.so_what: Full-stack AI-native plays trade operational complexity for full capture of value.

insights.claim: The author is convinced long-running agents will win the relay race at scale, expecting adoption in mortgage origination, insurance claims processing and complex enterprise sales, though it is too early to say which go-to-market approach prevails.
insights.speaker: David Haber
insights.so_what: Target verticals for agent disruption: mortgage, insurance claims, complex B2B sales.
